title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with mayonnaise is a popular dish often served at picnics, family lunches, and holiday tables. The basic ingredients are cooked pasta, mayonnaise, vegetables (such as peas, carrots, cucumbers) and seasonings. Its simplicity and rich flavor make it a favorite in many countries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pasta salad originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient picnic food.
Short-shaped pasta (rotini, penne, fusilli) is traditionally used because it holds the dressing well.
Regional variations add different ingredients: in Russia peas and carrots are common, while in Italy olives and Parmesan are added.
Mayonnaise can be substituted with yogurt or sour cream for a lighter version.
The salad keeps well in the fridge for 3‑4 days, but tastes best within the first 24 hours.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides energy through complex carbohydrates that are released slowly into the bloodstream.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Added vegetables (carrots, peas, cucumbers) enrich the salad with vitamins A, C, K and potassium.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Pasta and optional additions such as boiled chicken or eggs increase the protein content.

items.title: Probiotics (when using yogurt)
items.content: Replacing part of the mayo with natural yogurt introduces beneficial bacteria.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Peas and carrots add fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise is rich in saturated fats and calories; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Leaving the salad at room temperature for more than 2 hours can allow harmful bacteria to multiply.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Store‑bought mayo often contains a lot of salt; low‑sodium versions are better for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Regular pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives should be used for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish, alongside meat or fish, or use it as a filling for sandwiches and wraps. It travels well in a cooler or sealed container for picnics. Before serving, garnish with fresh herbs, paprika, or grated cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Stir before serving as the mayo may settle. Consume within 3‑4 days; discard if it develops an off‑odor or visible mold.
